title: Terraform AWS, Observability, and Interview Bridge
subtitle: Connect Terraform fluency to AWS, observability, data engineering, and interview-safe positioning

nodes.label: AWS Foundation
nodes.definition: AWS Foundation means the common cloud building blocks Terraform can define or standardize in AWS.
nodes.whyItMatters: Many cloud, data, platform, and observability roles expect awareness of how AWS resources are provisioned and governed.
nodes.safeSentence: Terraform can help define AWS foundation resources in a repeatable and reviewable way.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not imply deep AWS Terraform ownership if the actual experience is learning and collaboration-focused.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Terraform is commonly used to manage AWS foundation resources such as storage, IAM, networking, compute, and monitoring components. I am building fluency in how those pieces fit together.

note.summary: This map bridges Terraform ideas into AWS/data/observability conversations without overclaiming ownership.

image.caption: Terraform connects AWS foundation, observability, operations, and interview-safe communication.

nodes.label: S3
nodes.definition: S3 is AWS object storage commonly used for data, logs, exports, and lake-style storage.
nodes.whyItMatters: S3 is common in data engineering and observability workflows.
nodes.safeSentence: For data engineering, S3 is often a key storage layer that Terraform can help define consistently.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not create real buckets without naming, security, cost, and cleanup approval.
nodes.interviewAnswer: S3 is relevant because many data and logging workflows depend on durable object storage, and Terraform can help standardize bucket configuration.

note.summary: Terraform commonly defines bucket naming, tags, encryption, lifecycle, access, and logging settings.

nodes.label: IAM
nodes.definition: IAM controls AWS identities, roles, policies, and permissions.
nodes.whyItMatters: Terraform-managed infrastructure still needs secure access control.
nodes.safeSentence: IAM is critical because Terraform-managed infrastructure still needs secure access control.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not treat IAM as a copy/paste policy exercise. Permissions can create major security risk.
nodes.interviewAnswer: IAM matters because Terraform automation and cloud workloads need carefully scoped permissions, ideally following least privilege.

note.summary: IAM is high-risk: use least privilege, role-based access, separation by environment, and review of powerful permissions.

nodes.label: Networking
nodes.definition: Networking includes VPCs, subnets, security groups, routing, and connectivity boundaries.
nodes.whyItMatters: Cloud systems depend on network boundaries and connectivity.
nodes.safeSentence: Networking is one of the cloud areas where Terraform helps make infrastructure repeatable and reviewable.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not make networking changes casually; small changes can have broad impact.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Networking is important because applications, data pipelines, and monitoring systems all depend on connectivity and security boundaries.

note.summary: High-impact area: plan review and safety controls matter even for small config changes.

nodes.label: Compute
nodes.definition: Compute includes services that run workloads, such as EC2, ECS, EKS, Lambda, or other AWS execution platforms.
nodes.whyItMatters: Data pipelines, applications, and observability agents depend on compute.
nodes.safeSentence: Terraform can define the compute layer that applications, data pipelines, and monitoring tools depend on.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not talk as if all compute choices are the same; each has different operational and cost behavior.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Terraform can help define compute resources or supporting configuration, while operations teams still need monitoring, capacity, and cost visibility.

note.summary: Terraform defines shape; telemetry shows behavior; capacity planning checks sufficiency.

nodes.label: CloudWatch
nodes.definition: CloudWatch is AWS's native monitoring/logging/metrics service family.
nodes.whyItMatters: It connects AWS infrastructure to operational visibility.
nodes.safeSentence: Terraform can help define monitoring resources such as CloudWatch alarms or log groups.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not assume creating infrastructure is enough; monitoring and alerting must also be considered.
nodes.interviewAnswer: CloudWatch matters because AWS infrastructure needs logs, metrics, and alarms, and some of those observability assets can be managed as code.

note.summary: Terraform may manage log groups, alarms, dashboard config, and retention settings.

nodes.label: Observability Tools
nodes.definition: Observability tools collect and present signals such as logs, metrics, traces, dashboards, and alerts.
nodes.whyItMatters: Infrastructure changes need visibility after deployment.
nodes.safeSentence: Many observability platforms can be managed partly as code through Terraform providers.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not claim every observability setup is fully managed by Terraform.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Terraform can sometimes manage observability resources through providers, but the operational value comes from connecting infrastructure changes to telemetry, dashboards, and alerting.

note.summary: Good signal design and review still matter even with IaC-managed observability assets.

nodes.label: Dashboards as Code
nodes.definition: Dashboards as code means dashboard definitions are stored, reviewed, and managed like configuration.
nodes.whyItMatters: Dashboards become repeatable and easier to review instead of manual one-off screens.
nodes.safeSentence: Managing dashboards as code can make observability assets repeatable and easier to review.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not create dashboards with no owner, no purpose, or no action path.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Dashboards as code can help teams standardize operational views and reduce manual configuration drift.

note.summary: Ask who owns dashboard, what question it answers, and what action it should trigger.

nodes.label: Alerts as Code
nodes.definition: Alerts as code means alert rules are versioned, reviewed, and managed repeatably.
nodes.whyItMatters: Alert consistency helps teams detect issues without relying on manual console configuration.
nodes.safeSentence: Alerts as code help teams standardize monitoring thresholds and reduce manual configuration drift.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not create noisy alerts that nobody trusts.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Alerts as code can help standardize thresholds, ownership, routing, and review around monitoring changes.

note.summary: Good alerts need clear owner, threshold, runbook, and noise control.

nodes.label: Capacity Connection
nodes.definition: Capacity connection means Terraform defines infrastructure while capacity engineering studies whether that infrastructure has enough headroom.
nodes.whyItMatters: Provisioning and capacity planning should inform each other.
nodes.safeSentence: Terraform defines infrastructure, while capacity engineering studies whether that infrastructure has enough headroom for demand.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not confuse provisioning with forecasting. Terraform creates or changes infrastructure; capacity analysis studies behavior over time.
nodes.interviewAnswer: My capacity background helps me understand why infrastructure-as-code should be connected to telemetry, utilization, thresholds, and forward-looking planning.

note.summary: Bridge: Terraform asks what should exist; telemetry/capacity asks how it behaves and what to plan next.

nodes.label: Data Engineering Connection
nodes.definition: Data engineering connection means Terraform can define supporting cloud resources used by data pipelines.
nodes.whyItMatters: Data pipelines often depend on storage, IAM, compute, networking, and monitoring.
nodes.safeSentence: Data engineering pipelines often rely on infrastructure that can be provisioned or standardized through Terraform.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not claim Terraform replaces pipeline engineering; it supports the infrastructure around it.
nodes.interviewAnswer: For data engineering, Terraform is useful because pipelines often depend on cloud resources such as storage, IAM roles, compute, networking, and logging.

note.summary: Safe framing: understand resource dependencies even when platform teams own implementation.

nodes.label: Interview Bridge
nodes.definition: Interview Bridge is the safe story connecting Terraform learning to Sean's real background.
nodes.whyItMatters: It prevents overclaiming while still showing useful cloud/platform fluency.
nodes.safeSentence: My background is strongest in data, telemetry, monitoring, and capacity forecasting. Terraform helps me connect that operational experience to modern cloud infrastructure practices.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not say you owned enterprise Terraform production platforms if that is not true.
nodes.interviewAnswer: For my background, Terraform is valuable because it connects cloud infrastructure to the operational world I already know: monitoring, telemetry, capacity, dashboards, and risk. I am not claiming to be the main Terraform platform owner, but I understand the workflow and how it supports repeatable, safe cloud environments.

note.summary: Practice answer: Terraform workflow + state safety + data/telemetry/capacity bridge without overclaiming ownership.

nodes.label: Safety, Team Workflow, and CI/CD
nodes.definition: Open the previous map that explains safe Terraform team workflow.
nodes.whyItMatters: AWS and observability Terraform work must still follow review, plan, state, and apply controls.
nodes.safeSentence: AWS-facing Terraform work still needs safe team workflow and controlled change.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not treat this as an AWS concept. It is a map doorway.
nodes.interviewAnswer: The AWS/observability bridge only makes sense when connected to safe Terraform workflow: plan review, state protection, least privilege, and controlled apply.
